title: Scandi as WHITE!? Chase The Queen! | Sicilian, Smith-Morra | Top Theory Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: Recapturing with the queen isn't outright terrible, but it's misplaced here. Against a king's-pawn game this early queen sortie is the Center Game — genuinely playable. Against the Sicilian it's just poor, because it hands over a stack of tempi.

Why so many lost tempi? Because it amounts to playing a Scandinavian a move up as the wrong colour — and the Scandinavian is dubious enough that nobody wants it with either colour. Meanwhile the knight leaps out with gain of time, hitting the queen.

There are countless ways to arrange the pieces from here, and the guiding idea is to stay true to the spirit of whatever open-Sicilian repertoire you'd normally play — Dragon players reach for g6, Taimanov and Sveshnikov players for e6, Najdorf players for d6. All of them are valid.
In the spirit of the accelerated fianchetto, the bishop's diagonal comes first whenever there's no concrete reason to deviate — and here there's no downside to it.
The one thing to refuse is a trade of the fianchettoed bishop — swapping that piece off would be a real mistake, so the plan is simply to complete the setup around it.

That little pawn move is conceptually bad — it develops nothing and cramps its own knight. The opponent's development has fallen alarmingly behind, but that changes nothing on this side: just keep bringing pieces out, with a d5 break in the back pocket for when the moment to open the centre arrives.
Keep developing — the knight comes to f6. The trap to avoid is the very error the opponent fell into: dragging the queen out too early.

This looks like it contradicts the usual advice to play e6 and g7 so as not to block the dark-squared bishop — but it's a different situation, and knowing the difference is proper use of comparison. Here the bishop isn't the centre of the universe; speed and cracking the centre open are. The e6-and-g7 plan costs two moves, while the knight leap is efficient, active, and leans on the e-pawn.
The knight on f6 is doing real work — efficient, active, and pressing the e4-pawn. It's still too early for the central break; there's a useful move to insert first.
That move is castling — just tuck the king away. The opponent is nowhere near finishing development, so there's plenty of time to spend a safety move first.

The push overextends a position with no pieces out — the train left the tracks long ago. And a general rule fires here: whenever a pawn advances, it mathematically vacates a square. Always know which square just opened and whether a piece can seize it.

The vacated square invites the knight to centralise on d5 — keeping the piece in the middle where its reach is greatest, in line with the principle. The rim square works too, but central posting is the cleaner choice.

Now a lesson in resisting one-move-itis: recapture the pawn with the knight, not the bishop. Taking with the knight sets up a fork on d3 and keeps the exposed queen pinned to its awkward post. Grabbing with the bishop hands the queen a route back to safety — and pulling a fianchettoed bishop off its diagonal, even along the same line, invites the opponent to develop with tempo and offer the trade you least want.

Rather than the obvious queen thrust, a subtler post is better — and it passes the honest test for whether a move is a mere trick: would you still play it if the threat vanished? Yes — the queen here eyes the c3-pawn should the opponent castle long, and helps knit the rooks together. That it also threatens to win the queen is a bonus, not the whole point.
And the trick cashes in — a knight check on d3 wins the queen outright.

Up a queen, the right instinct isn't to snatch more pawns but to open the position before the opponent ever finishes developing. So don't dawdle with d6 — throw in d5, gift a pawn, and blow the d-file wide open. Speed is worth more than a pawn here.
Knowing when to grab material and when to give it back is an art, not a science. The direct route to the loose knight is to reroute the dark-squared bishop up to h6.

A careful amendment: the natural pin would let the king slip to the corner, and then a recapture keeps everything defended. So instead, plant the bishop on f5 to freeze the king in place — a target that can't move is far easier to hunt down — while readying the last rook to join.

The cleanest finish uses the pin instead of the greedy capture: the queen steps to e4, and because the enemy knight is pinned to its king, both squares it seems to guard are an illusion. Mate follows on the back rank — the pure power of the pin.

The takeaway when a combination like this feels invisible: it's usually because the pin is being underestimated and the eye is glued to the free piece. Train the habit — every time a piece hangs, spend an extra fifteen or twenty seconds weighing the quieter candidate moves before grabbing it.

To be fair about the theory — against a king's-pawn game this same queen recapture is the respectable Center Game, played even at the top level as an offbeat try. It's only against the Sicilian that it sinks to the bottom tier; there the queen really ought to stay planted in the centre.
